newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnian cabinet adopts customs law -- officials.
newsitem.headline: Bosnian cabinet adopts customs law -- officials.

text.p: Members of the Bosnian central cabinet said they adopted a draft customs law on Thursday, moving the country a step closer to clinching a post-war agreement with the International Monetary Fund.
The co-chairman of the Council of Ministers, Haris Silajdzic, told state radio that the law was a temporary measure until a more comprehensive reform could be drafted.
"It will be effective for a period of six months and then we will meet again and negotiate," he said.
The customs law is part of a package of economic reforms which the peacetime Bosnian government needs to adopt to obtain an agreement with the IMF.
Foreign experts said most of the necessary legislative package had been adopted or was close to adoption after the collective presidency agreed a draft central bank law late on Wednesday.
The economic reforms also pave the way for an international donors' conference which is expected to raise some $1.4 billion in reconstruction aid.
Silajdzic said the donors' conference might be held in the second half of June.
Bosnian ministers reached a compromise on the customs law, which calculated customs rates based on an average of rates in the country's autonomous Serb and Moslem-Croat territories.

They decided against adopting a more ambitious customs reform drawn up by international consultants. This would have created separate rates for raw materials, finished goods and semi-finished goods, said a foreign expert who asked not to be named.
Bosnian officials discarded the proposal partly because they feared it could reduce budget revenues in the Moslem-Croat federation and the Serb entity, the expert said.
The draft law calls for more than 20 customs rates and should not significantly alter revenues for the Serb or Moslem-Croat entities.
Foreign experts said it was only one of many measures needed by Bosnia to revive trade after a devastating war.

Although much of the transport network has been repaired by NATO engineers since fighting ended in 1995, political haggling between rival nationalist leaders has prevented the reopening of railways and many roads linking the two entities.
Michael Steiner, deputy to the international High Representative to Bosnia, said the customs law proved that the Moslem, Serb and Croat representatives in the cabinet could work efficiently.
"I think what has been shown is that this institution, if the political will is there, can do its work and do it well," Steiner told Bosnian radio.
